newsitem.title: USA: NYC bar, ABA near agreement on pay-to-play policy.
newsitem.headline: NYC bar, ABA near agreement on pay-to-play policy.

text.p: New York City lawyers and the American Bar Association are close to an agreement on a draft voluntary policy to curb pay-to-play by the nation's lawyers, an ABA official said Friday.
The push for an agreement is on because ABA delegates are scheduled to vote on the issue at their annual meeting set for July 30 to August 6 in San Francisco.

"The draft ... is now reaching the point where someone can say 'We've got it'," Raymond Trombadore, chairman of ABA's standing committee on professional discipline, said in a telephone interview. "We're coming very close."
Trombadore said that an ABA ad hoc panel studying the issue will send written comments on the latest draft to the Association of the Bar of the City of New York today.

ABA's ad hoc committee and New York City's bar are currently "playing ping-pong" with the drafts, Trombadore said, noting that the latest City bar plan came in July 15. He said the two versions are close and undergoing fine tuning.
Trombadore said the latetst draft condemns pay-to-play by any lawyer providing services to public agencies and makes clear that ABA rules prohibit attorneys from the practice.

He said the draft urges state lawmakers and regulators to adopt standards barring pay-to-play and to enforce those requirements. It also calls for a new task force to recommend within 12 months whether further action is needed, he said.
The draft policy urges bar associations, lawyer disciplinary agencies, and courts to enforce existing rules of professional conduct on the issue, such as ABA's model rule 7.1(c), Trombadore said.
Rule 7.1(c) prohibits lawyers from giving "anything of value" to someone for recommending the lawyer's services.
Pay-to-play refers to bond professionals who give contributions to elected municipal officials in return for bond business, or even to be considered for bond business.

Wall Street bond dealers four years ago signed a voluntary pact banning pay-to-play among their ranks. The New York City bar last year voted to bar muni lawyers that give to muni clients from doing bond business for two years with those governments.
Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt has aggressively pushed bond lawyers, who are not directly regulated by SEC, to do the same.
